## Diagnosis
Yes, it is past fine: the plumber's second truck, "That number is the price of laptops," the henhouse sections shipping assembled, and the fourth check applied to a Forbes vice president are all sentences a reader will repeat to someone else, which is the only test that matters. What holds it back is a reflex that shows up maybe a dozen times — the draft lands a dry fact, then adds a following clause that tells the reader what the fact just did, and the clause spends the laugh the fact had already earned. The related tic is the hedge in front position ("For the most part," "In most cases," "may claim"), which apologizes for a flat sentence before the sentence gets to be flat.

## Suggestions
### 1
Original: For the most part, the companies making money from AI were not the companies making announcements about it.
Replacement: The companies making money from AI were not the companies making announcements about it.
Buys: The section's opening line stops apologizing for itself three words before it lands.

### 2
Original: Those nouns can be swapped, as the noun does no actual work.
Replacement: CUT
Buys: The swap test in the next sentence is the joke; stating the verdict first pays it out before the reader can.

### 3
Original: If these ideas are so easily debunked, why do so many of them survive contact with senior management?
Replacement: The ideas are easy to debunk. They survive senior management anyway.
Buys: Removes a one-line question paragraph — the piece's most generic move — and the answers that follow arrive as answers rather than as a quiz key.

### 4
Original: CTO Andrew Bosworth answered that the time should actually serve the users and publicly questioned the employee's approach to their career in front of the entire gathering, later calling his remark humorous [23].
Replacement: CTO Andrew Bosworth answered that the time should serve the users, then questioned the employee's approach to their career in front of the whole Q&A. He later called the remark humorous [23].
Buys: Cuts the redundancy of "publicly... in front of the entire gathering" and moves the best fact in the anecdote to end position, where it works unassisted.

### 5
Original: A slide may claim an opportunity runs into the trillions, but whose revenue does that number actually describe? In most cases the answer is nobody's.
Replacement: A slide claims the opportunity runs into the trillions. The trillions are nobody's revenue.
Buys: Two flat statements instead of a hedged question and its own answer; the sentence after it already supplies the proof, so the question was doing no work.

### 6
Original: Ten years have found me responsible for AI strategy in production systems, which mostly means I am the one who must state what a plan will cost and who will actually pay for it, and I write every article with AI assistance, spending hours each week extracting prose that looks finished from these models.
Replacement: Ten years have found me responsible for AI strategy in production systems, which mostly means I am the one who states what a plan will cost and who pays for it. I also write every article with AI assistance, spending hours each week extracting prose that looks finished from these models.
Buys: Fifty words carrying two separate credentials become two sentences, so the second admission is heard instead of trailing the first.

## Paragraph move
Move the "Ask twice, in two different meetings" paragraph up so it sits directly after "These are ordinary questions asked in good faith to be helpful," before the Bosworth anecdote. As written it is procedural advice placed after the section's payoff, so the closing beat of the whole argument is a caveat about bad days and poorly phrased questions rather than "before the year you would have spent executing it." Relocated, it reads as part of the instruction for how to ask, and the Bosworth receipt plus the price-of-one-question line close the section on its strongest two sentences and hand off cleanly to the locked ending.
